sized-numbers.comment: Verilog-style sized literal (`8'd6`/`8'hFF`/`8'b1010`/`8'o17`/`8'6`, see src/lexer.rs's SizedInt token) — listed BEFORE #numbers so `8` isn't matched as a bare number first, leaving `'d6` to fall through to #operators (`'`)/#identifiers (`d6`).
sized-numbers.name: constant.numeric.trace

declarations-with-name.comment: module/rule/struct NAME — highlighted as a unit so the declared name reads as a type/function, not a plain identifier.

patterns.comment: Verse-spelled prefix logical negation, replacing the old symbolic `!` — a real lexer keyword (src/lexer.rs), highlighted as an operator since that's how it functions.
patterns.name: keyword.operator.word.trace

patterns.comment: Verse's failure-discharging fallback chain (`A or B or C`) — a real lexer keyword (src/lexer.rs), highlighted as an operator like `not` above since that's how it functions.
patterns.name: keyword.operator.word.trace

patterns.comment: `schedule` itself is matched by #schedule-block instead (a real lexer keyword, so no ambiguity risk there — see that rule's own comment), which needs to consume it as part of opening its own scoped region.
patterns.name: keyword.declaration.trace

patterns.comment: uN (u8, u32, ...) is sugar for bits[N] — see src/parser.rs's u_width, same treatment as `bit` above.
patterns.name: keyword.declaration.trace

literals.comment: `false` spells the absent value of a `?T` (Verse's logic-programming-flavored `none`, see src/lexer.rs's TokenKind::False) — a real lexer keyword, not a general boolean (no `true` counterpart).
literals.name: constant.language.trace

effect-words.comment: Contextual identifiers, not lexer keywords (see src/lexer.rs) — legal as ordinary identifiers everywhere else, so only included from inside #effects-list, never matched bare at the top level (unlike the schedule-directive words below, these can't be scoped by a real keyword the way `schedule` itself can, since there's no unambiguous bracket to anchor on other than the `<...>` this rule lives inside). Known accepted collision: a state name inside the `{...}` argument list of `reads {...}`/`writes {...}` that happens to match one of these words (e.g. `reads {reads}`) highlights as an effect keyword instead of a plain identifier — fixing it would need a dedicated nested region for just that `{...}`, disproportionate for a cosmetic mismatch confined to one token.
effect-words.name: keyword.other.effect.trace

schedule-directives.comment: Contextual identifiers too, same as #effect-words — only included from inside #schedule-block, never matched bare at the top level.
schedule-directives.name: keyword.other.effect.trace

effects-list.comment: `<...>` effects tag list. Begins only when `<` is immediately followed by a known effect word — `<` is also the less-than operator (#operators), and this language has no generics to otherwise disambiguate against, so a bare `<` alone can't safely open a region (a runaway match to some unrelated later `>` would be far more confusing than the imprecision this rule fixes). `end` additionally stops at end-of-line as a defensive cap: every real effects list is written on one line in practice, so even the rare adversarial case (`x < reads`, a variable actually named `reads`) can't cascade highlighting past that one line.

schedule-block.comment: `schedule { ... }`. `schedule` is a real lexer keyword (src/lexer.rs), unlike the directive words inside it, so anchoring on it carries no ambiguity risk the way #effects-list's `<` does. #schedule-body recurses on its own nested `{ }` (mutually_exclusive/conflict_free's own name lists), so this correctly scopes to the WHOLE block regardless of that inner nesting, not just up to the first `}`.

calls.comment: identifier( — covers both calls and fn/spec/impl declarations, which have no leading keyword in this language.
calls.name: entity.name.function.trace
